clinicalPearls: Respiratory distress in a newborn born through meconium-stained amniotic fluid, when meconium is aspirated into the airways around the time of birth.
It occurs mainly in term and post-term infants and is associated with fetal distress and intrauterine hypoxia.
Affected infants may be meconium-stained, have distress from birth with tachypnoea and recession, and show a barrel-shaped, hyperinflated chest.
The chest radiograph typically shows patchy or coarse infiltrates with areas of hyperinflation and atelectasis, and air leaks are common.
Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn frequently complicates the syndrome and contributes to severe hypoxaemia.
Routine intrapartum suctioning of the airway and routine tracheal suction of vigorous meconium-stained infants are no longer recommended.
Non-vigorous infants born through meconium may need resuscitation, and management is largely supportive with oxygen and respiratory support.
Severe cases may require mechanical ventilation, surfactant, inhaled nitric oxide for pulmonary hypertension, and occasionally extracorporeal membrane oxygenation.
Air leaks such as pneumothorax and pneumomediastinum are important and potentially sudden complications.
reference.pathophysiology: Intrauterine stress and hypoxia can provoke passage of meconium into the amniotic fluid and gasping that draws it into the airways. Aspirated meconium causes mechanical airway obstruction with a ball-valve effect producing air trapping and air leaks, a chemical pneumonitis with inflammation, and inactivation of surfactant. These changes cause ventilation-perfusion mismatch and hypoxaemia, and, combined with hypoxia-driven pulmonary vasoconstriction, promote persistent pulmonary hypertension with right-to-left shunting.
additionalDifferentials: Respiratory distress syndrome (in less mature infants)
Persistent pulmonary hypertension from other causes
additionalInvestigations: Chest radiograph for patchy infiltrates, hyperinflation, and air leaks
Pulse oximetry (pre- and post-ductal) and blood gas analysis
Echocardiography to assess for pulmonary hypertension
Sepsis screen when infection cannot be excluded
redFlags: Severe or refractory hypoxaemia despite respiratory support
Large pre- to post-ductal saturation gradient suggesting pulmonary hypertension
Sudden deterioration indicating pneumothorax or other air leak
Signs of hypoxic-ischaemic injury to other organs
reference.prognosis: Most infants with mild to moderate disease recover with supportive care, but severe disease complicated by persistent pulmonary hypertension or air leaks carries significant morbidity and mortality; survivors may have transient respiratory sequelae.
pitfalls: Performing routine intrapartum or tracheal suctioning that is no longer recommended
Underestimating the risk of pneumothorax and missing a sudden air leak
Failing to recognise coexisting persistent pulmonary hypertension
Overlooking associated hypoxic-ischaemic injury to other organs
Delaying escalation of respiratory support in rapidly deteriorating infants
management: Respiratory support graded to severity, from supplemental oxygen and CPAP to mechanical ventilation
Exogenous surfactant replacement, or surfactant lavage, to counter meconium-induced surfactant inactivation
Treat persistent pulmonary hypertension with inhaled nitric oxide, optimal oxygenation and avoidance of acidosis
Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation for refractory hypoxaemic respiratory failure
Vigilance for and prompt drainage of air leaks such as pneumothorax
Empirical antibacterials when sepsis cannot be excluded, alongside continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring and supportive neonatal intensive care
Follow current resuscitation guidance that no longer recommends routine intrapartum or tracheal suctioning of vigorous meconium-stained infants
